summary:
What We Developed:
We developed FIRE HARMONIX, an interactive geospatial intelligence platform that tracks historical (2020–2026) and real-time active fire events across India. By unifying 3,518,726 satellite records into a single web dashboard, the platform features a 365-Day Burning Activity Heatmap Calendar filterable from All India down to individual districts, a high-speed Google Satellite & OpenStreetMap viewer, automated surge banners, and one-click CSV exports.
How It Addresses the Challenge:
Raw satellite feeds from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS sensors suffer from differing spatial resolutions, scan-angle distortion, and duplicate detections of the same fire. FIRE HARMONIX resolves these cross-sensor discrepancies into one unified Harmonized Fire Activity Index (HFAI) while replacing massive, slow spreadsheets with a single-screen annual calendar and live 4-sensor satellite tracking.
Why It Is Important:
During peak wildfire and agricultural burning seasons, forest departments and disaster managers lose critical hours interpreting fragmented files. FIRE HARMONIX gives responders an instant visual overview of seasonal burn windows and abnormal fire surges so they can deploy resources in seconds. Additionally, district-level tracking of crop residue burning helps policymakers curb severe seasonal air pollution before toxic smoke plumes impact millions of urban residents—democratizing NASA Earth observation data without requiring specialized GIS software.
details:
FIRE HARMONIX brings together 3.51 million historical NASA fire records (2020–2026) and live satellite alerts into one simple, easy-to-use website for India. Instead of making people dig through complicated spreadsheets or conflicting maps, it gives users a single-screen 365-Day Burning Activity Calendar linked to a live Satellite Map—allowing anyone to explore fire trends from All India down to a single district and download clean reports in one click.

How It Works:

• 1. Balancing Two Different Satellites: NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellites capture fires at different camera sizes and resolutions. Our system adjusts their measurements onto one fair, equal scale so both satellites can be compared accurately.

• 2. Removing Optical Errors: Satellites sometimes pick up false heat signals at the far edges of their camera view. Our physics filter automatically cleans out these false readings before showing anything on the map.

• 3. Merging Duplicate Sightings: When both satellites spot the exact same fire on the same day, our system merges them into one single point, so the same fire is never counted twice.

• 4. Scoring & Finding the Cause: Every verified fire gets a simple 0 to 100 severity score (HFAI). When you click on any fire dot, our smart diagnostic tool checks its heat intensity and location to help tell whether it is a dangerous forest wildfire or seasonal crop burning.

• 5. Instant Surge Alerts & Fast Loading: By comparing today’s live satellite feeds against seven years of past data, the platform flashes immediate Green, Yellow, or Red warning banners when fire activity spikes abnormally loading millions of records in less than a second on any regular laptop or phone.

What Benefits Does It Have?

• Helps Officials Make Faster Decisions: Instead of showing plain red dots with no explanation, FIRE HARMONIX helps forest rangers and disaster teams quickly see whether a hotspot is an urgent forest wildfire or routine crop burning—making it clear when to send firefighting teams or enforce air-quality rules.

• Stops Wasted Time on False Alarms: Satellites often mistake sunlight reflection, solar panels, or hot factory roofs for fires. By filtering out false heat signals using basic heat physics, our system saves emergency crews from chasing false alarms.

• Spots Danger Early Using 7 Years of History: Looking at today’s map alone cannot tell you if fire numbers are normal or starting to spiral out of control. Comparing live alerts against 3.51 million past records (2020–2026) warns authorities early before small fires grow into major disasters.

• Protects Public Health from Smoke Pollution: Tracking crop-residue burning district by district gives local leaders an early warning so they can step in before heavy smoke spreads to nearby cities and harms millions of people.

• Works on Any Device Without Expensive Software: Most satellite analysis requires costly mapping software and hours of manual work. FIRE HARMONIX runs smoothly in any standard web browser on a regular laptop or phone, letting researchers and local officials download verified reports in one click.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software We Used:

• Data Harmonization & Model Training (Google Colab): We used Google Colab to download raw multi-year datasets from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellites, process each year individually, harmonize them into one unified dataset, build our 365-day calendar baselines, and train our fire-scoring model.

• Coding Languages: We used Python for data harmonization, model training, and backend logic, along with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interactive calendar and map interface.

• Development & Version Control Software: We used Visual Studio Code (VS Code) to build and test the full web application, and used Git and GitHub (pulling, pushing, and hosting our large database via GitHub Releases) to manage our code.

• Backend, Database & Mapping Tools: We used Pandas and NumPy for data processing, SQLite to store and index 3.51 million harmonized records, Fast API and Uvicorn to run the server, NASA FIRMS API for live alerts, Leaflet.js (with OpenStreetMap and Google Satellite layers) for mapping, and Render.com for live cloud hosting.

What Makes FIRE HARMONIX Uniquely Creative

• 1. Fusing Two Orbital Eyes into One Scientific Language (HFAI): Rather than forcing users to switch between conflicting MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) maps, we creatively combined Stefan–Boltzmann pixel-area scaling (2.667x), View Zenith Angle (VZA) bowtie filtering, and 1.0 km Haversine deduplication into a single 0–100 Harmonized Fire Activity Index (HFAI) so both satellites speak one unified physical language.

• 2. Giving Satellites a with a Click-to-Decision Engine: Instead of plotting silent red dots that leave humans guessing, our diagnostic engine evaluates Fire Radiative Power (FRP), thermal brightness, and land-use context to classify why a fire is burning—separating urgent forest wildfires from seasonal crop-residue burning alongside non-parametric Modified Z-Score (MAD) surge alerts.

• 3. A Zero-Scroll "365-Day Burning Calendar" Synced to a Live Map: Rather than burying 3.51 million rows in massive spreadsheets, we designed a single-screen 12-month color-graded heatmap calendar linked directly to a 60fps Leaflet Canvas satellite map, letting anyone travel across seven years (2020–2026) and zoom from All India down to a single district in one glance.

• 4. Pocket-Supercomputing on Everyday Hardware: Processing 3,518,726 multi-year records usually demands expensive cloud clusters. By pairing 6 composite B-Tree SQLite indexes, 0.05° spatial grid cells, and an in-memory calendar cache with parallel 4-sensor NASA FIRMS polling, we engineered a lightweight browser app that delivers < 1 ms calendar lookups and < 70 ms map queries on any basic laptop or phone.

Key Design Factors & Engineering Milestones Our Team Considered:

• Mastering Multi-Year Big Data at Scale: Handling and harmonizing over 3.51 million active fire records across multiple years (2020–2026) from two completely different orbital sensors (MODIS and VIIRS) is normally a heavy supercomputing task. Our team engineered a lightweight, unified harmonizing model (HFAI) and indexed SQLite architecture that processes years of multi-sensor satellite history in milliseconds on standard hardware.

• Turning Satellites into a Real-Time Decision Co-Pilot: Raw satellite alerts are useless if local officials do not know how to act on them. We designed FIRE HARMONIX not just as a data viewer, but as an intelligent decision-support companion—translating complex radiative physics (Stefan–Boltzmann scaling and FRP thresholds) into clear, human-readable diagnoses that separate urgent forest wildfires from seasonal agricultural burns.

• Statistical Robustness Against Fat-Tail Spikes: Because peak crop-burning weeks create massive statistical outliers, we chose median-based MAD Z-scores over standard means, so historical baselines remain trustworthy.

• 60fps Responsiveness Across Devices: We partitioned coordinates into 0.05° (5.5 km) spatial grid cells and used Abort Controller-guarded browser fetches so thousands of points render smoothly on both classroom projectors and mobile devices.
